sentences.text: Welcome to Interactive Lab 1! On Canvas 1, toggle between Git commit versions v1.0, v1.1, and v2.0 to observe how lightweight .dvc pointer files swap multi-gigabyte datasets in zero milliseconds. On Canvas 2, inspect the storage deduplication chart to see how Content-Addressable Storage and reflinks save over sixty-seven percent disk storage compared to naive copying!
Let's explore the Git-DVC dual-tracking workbench! Switch between dataset versions on Canvas 1 to inspect hash pointer binding, and verify the storage deduplication ratio on Canvas 2.

Active Checkpoint 1! A researcher packages a 1.8 gigabyte dataset file with MD5 hash b7e21a4f08c3d9a6b1e5f8a2c7d4e3f1. Determine the exact remote S3 object path under DVC two-character sharding, specify what Git tracks, and describe what command an engineer must run on another workstation to materialize the actual data.
First checkpoint! How does DVC partition MD5 hashes in Content-Addressable Storage, and what happens when an engineer checks out the Git repository on a remote machine?

Flawless CAS resolution! Option B is correct. Under Definition 13.9.2, DVC shards hashes by taking the first two hex characters as the directory prefix and the remaining thirty characters as the object name: s3://bucket/dvc-cache/b7/e21a4f08c3d9a6b1e5f8a2c7d4e3f1. Git only tracks the tiny eighty-byte .dvc pointer file, so running dvc checkout or dvc pull is required to materialize the data via zero-copy hardlinks or reflinks!

Incorrect. Option B is correct. DVC shards the 32-character hash into a 2-character prefix directory (b7) and a 30-character filename. Git only tracks the tiny 80-byte pointer manifest, meaning git checkout does not download the binary; running dvc checkout or dvc pull is required.

Welcome to Interactive Lab 2! On Canvas 1, test DVC pipeline stage key memoization: click Modify paper.qmd to observe stages 1 through 3 hitting cache in zero seconds while only stage 4 re-renders. On Canvas 2, observe the notebook execution entropy gauge and transition matrix, comparing erratic out-of-order execution against the linear zero-entropy Quarto invariant.
Let's test pipeline memoization and notebook entropy! Trigger selective DAG invalidation on Canvas 1, and watch how erratic cell execution spikes entropy on Canvas 2.

Active Checkpoint 2! Consider a 4-stage DVC pipeline: Stage 1 takes 600s, Stage 2 takes 300s, Stage 3 takes 1,800s, and Stage 4 takes 60s. If a researcher only modifies the narrative introduction in paper.qmd without altering upstream data or hyperparameters, compute the total runtime under DVC repro and evaluate the computational speedup factor.
Second checkpoint! How does DVC stage memoization handle changes to downstream document templates, and what speedup factor does it achieve over full recomputation?

Outstanding pipeline memoization analysis! Option C is correct. Because upstream inputs, code, and hyperparameters are unaltered, Stages 1, 2, and 3 have identical stage execution keys and hit cache in zero seconds. Only Stage 4 executes for 60 seconds. Naive full execution takes 2,760 seconds, so DVC achieves an exact 46.0 times computational speedup factor!

That's not right. Option C is correct. Stages 1 through 3 find their stage execution keys identical to dvc.lock, bypassing execution in 0 seconds. Only Stage 4 runs for 60 seconds. Comparing naive runtime of 2,760 seconds against 60 seconds yields a 46.0x speedup factor.

Active Checkpoint 3! In computational science, published Jupyter notebooks frequently fail to reproduce reported metrics despite identical cell code and data. Based on Definition 13.9.4 and Theorem 13.9.2, identify the mathematical root cause and describe how headless literate compilers guarantee reproducibility.
Final checkpoint! Why do interactive notebooks suffer from hidden state pollution, and how does headless linear compilation solve it?

Masterclass systems diagnosis! Option A is correct. Interactive cell execution follows an arbitrary non-linear permutation trajectory with positive execution entropy: H of E greater than zero. This mutates global kernel state and leaves ghost variables in memory. Headless publication engines enforce the Linear Execution Invariant: executing cells strictly in ascending order from a fresh unpolluted kernel, driving entropy to zero bits and guaranteeing bitwise reproducibility!

Incorrect. Option A is correct. Out-of-order execution in interactive notebooks creates hidden in-memory state mutations where execution entropy H of E is positive. Headless compilation enforces the Linear Execution Invariant, evaluating cells strictly from top to bottom on a clean kernel so H of E equals zero.
